title: Giant Stone Heads Lie Face-Up On A Turkish Mountain

basis.note: median of recent videos blended with the niche benchmark; learning gated until day 5

predicted_range.basis: about 3x either way, from backtested error (249 of our own videos so far)

segments.narration: Giant stone heads lie face-up on a Turkish mountain. Over two thousand metres up Nemrut, broken off statues that once stood nine metres tall.
King Antiochus of Commagene built this tomb-sanctuary in 62 BC: himself, two lions, two eagles, and gods who were half Greek, half Persian.
Behind the terraces rises a cone of loose rubble, forty-nine metres high. And the king's grave? Still missing.
That rubble is why. Dig into loose rock and the hole pours shut behind you, and archaeologists think that was the entire design.
A German engineer, Karl Sester, excavated here in 1881. Nearly a century and a half later, Antiochus is still somewhere inside his own mountain.

verdicts.claim: Mount Nemrut stands at about 2,134 m and its statues, originally 8-9 m tall, now have their heads detached and scattered across the site.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia's infobox gives 2,134 m (the body text gives 2,150 m, so the narration says 'over two thousand metres'), statues of 8-9 m, and heads removed and now scattered throughout the site.

verdicts.claim: King Antiochus I of Commagene built the mountaintop tomb-sanctuary in 62 BC, with statues of himself, two lions, two eagles and composite Greek-Iranian gods.

verdicts.claim: The tumulus is 49 m tall and 152 m in diameter and the tomb of Antiochus I has never been found.

verdicts.claim: Archaeologists suggest the loose-rock tumulus was built so that any excavation would quickly fill in, protecting the tomb from robbers.
